newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S. bombers head to Gulf for expected Iraq raid.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bombers head to Gulf for expected Iraq raid.

text.p: U.S. stealth fighter-bombers headed to the Gulf on Thursday for what seemed almost certain retaliation against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein for a missile attack on U.S. warplanes patrolling over Iraq.
U.S. officials said Washington sought and received permission for the use of ground facilities in Kuwait.
But Kuwaiti officials would not confirm that eight F-117A stealths had arrived in the oil state at the head of the Gulf.
In Baghdad, Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz sharply warned Kuwait against permitting U.S. warplanes to use its territory for possible strikes against Iraq, saying the move was an act of war.
"We consider this conduct on the part of the Kuwaiti regime a flagrant aggression against Iraq and an act of war against the state of Iraq," he said in a statement.

Kuwait, grateful for its liberation from occupying Iraqi troops by a U.S.-led coalition in 1991, is the only Arab country to have expressed understanding for two U.S. missile attacks on Iraq last week.
The raids on air defence targets in southern Iraq, in which several Iraqis were killed and others wounded, drew international condemnation.
Senior Kuwaiti ministers, military officers and members of the Supreme Defence Council met on Thursday to discuss the growing tension.

A source close to the government told Reuters they discussed "plans and preparations on all sectors of the military...and also reviewed the political contacts with friendly and brotherly states and accords signed with them...An official statement will be issued shortly."

Kuwait state radio said Crown Prince and Prime Minister Sheikh Saad al-Abdulla al-Sabah, who chaired the meeting, told those present to "stay alert and cautious to handle all possibilities to guarantee the security of the state and its stability to safeguard it from all dangers and secure the safety of citizens".

U.S. defence officials said the stealth aircraft, which are designed to elude enemy radar, could be used at night to drop laser-guided bombs on Iraqi command and control centres if President Bill Clinton ordered new strikes.
Four long-range B-52 bombers like those used in last week's U.S. attacks on Iraqi air defence sites have been brought forward to within closer striking range of Iraqi targets.
They flew from Guam in the Pacific Ocean to a British airbase on the Indian Ocean island of Diego Garcia.
U.S. warships in the Gulf and B-52s launched 44 Tomahawk and airborne cruise missiles in two raids last week to punish Saddam for using his forces to attack Kurds in northern Iraq.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said Iraq's missile attack on two F-16 fighters policing a no-fly zone in northern Iraq on Wednesday would draw a "disproportionate" American response.

Saudi Arabia, the United States' chief strategic ally in the Middle East, main base for U.S. forces in the Gulf and launch pad for the Gulf War against Iraq, on Wednesday broke more than a week's silence after the raids.
Saudi Defence and Aviation Minister Prince Sultan said in Riyadh: "This (the use of the bases) was not requested from us. If it was requested we would have rejected it."

Saudi Arabia and other Gulf Arab states depend on U.S. protection from any external threat, but Riyadh is highly sensitive to publicity about the U.S. presence in the kingdom, where two bomb attacks have killed 24 Americans and two Indians in the past year.
Washington has made clear its strategic interests lie not with the Kurds in the north but in Saddam's potential threat to oil interests in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.
